reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because it presents Chegg as an educational question-answering service where participants may receive stated per-question payment. The subject test, training guidance, document verification, and expert registration form are described as recruitment or onboarding steps, while the opening payout overlays do not establish a guaranteed amount or deception.

opening.argument: Judge the income claim together with the action it solicits. The speaker says students can cover monthly expenses through the platform, then directs viewers into registration: “click on services, experts. Q&A and” “then click on this button called join now and then login.” The pathway continues through tests and document verification before the viewer “should. Be able to earn money.” That is an earnings pitch tied to joining and submitting information, not merely a discussion of an educational service. The later monthly calculation gives the pitch a concrete payoff, while the video does not establish that a newly registered viewer will receive one payable question every day.

rebuttal.rebuttal: Calling these steps ordinary onboarding does not settle what the pitch promises. The speaker connects completing verification to being able to earn, then presents a monthly-expense outcome calculated from daily paid work. The explanation of how questions are answered does not show that such work will be available to the viewer at that frequency. The concern is the solicitation created by pairing a concrete income prospect with registration and document submission, not that a subject test is inherently suspicious.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The argument turns a conditional example into a promise of available work. The speaker says payment follows a proper answer and explicitly makes the monthly total depend on answering one question per day. The test, training, and verification are presented as requirements for subject-matter work, not as a shortcut to free cash. Nothing cited shows a deceptive registration flow or a guaranteed monthly payment.

opening.argument: The presentation repeatedly centers the payout: it opens with “APPS THAT PAY,” asks viewers to watch for the “EXACT PAYOUT,” and leads with a friend's claim that the earnings cover all monthly expenses. Later, the speaker calls the questions “a piece of cake” for many viewers and calculates 5040 rupees from one answer a day. Together, those cues make the income sound both accessible and sufficient, even though the calculation depends on a steady stream of accepted answers that the video does not demonstrate. The risk is not the existence of educational questions; it is how confidently an easy-income outcome is promoted from an anecdote and a hypothetical.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense is right that a payout overlay alone proves no guarantee. But the concern rests on the combined framing: “a piece of cake” lowers the perceived effort, while the worked monthly figure invites viewers to treat one paid answer per day as a practical plan. Saying the figure is conditional does not establish that the condition is realistic for a new participant. Nor does describing the service as educational verify the opening anecdote about covering expenses.

Attention-grabbing payout language may oversimplify the opportunity, but these citations do not show a false payout or a reward for merely signing up.

opening.argument: This is framed as a walkthrough, but its destination matters. The speaker starts with a friend's monthly-expense story, tells viewers they too can earn, and moves directly to “join now” and login. The screen then shows a registration form collecting personal details, followed by a workflow that includes document verification. Explaining what an educational platform does lends credibility to a pitch whose practical instruction is to enter its recruitment process. The video shows the route into that process much more concretely than it shows actual completed work or payment to a new viewer. A judge should assess the income-led participation push, not just the instructional format.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense identifies the platform's stated purpose, but that does not answer the promotional structure. The speaker tells viewers how to reach the expert registration flow and says verification precedes the ability to earn. Those steps may be legitimate onboarding; the point is that the educational explanation also serves an income-driven call to participate. The cited walkthrough establishes the sign-up path, while the claimed monthly-expense result remains an anecdote and projection.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Promotion does not by itself make an instructional video a scam. The speaker describes the work as resolving students' questions, makes payment conditional on a proper answer, and walks through a test, training, and verification. The cited registration screen shows a recruitment form, not evidence that information is misused. The wrong-side argument correctly observes a call to join, but it supplies no evidence that the opportunity or its payment terms are deceptive.
